title: CVT in the Peripartum Period: A Diagnostic Dilemma
journal: Case Reports in Obstetrics and Gynecology
case_prompt: A 23-year-old woman, gravida 3 para 2, presented with a severe, continuous frontal headache and neck stiffness immediately after a difficult epidural analgesia for vaginal delivery (four attempts). On postpartum day 1, an anesthesiology consultation led to an epidural blood patch despite headache lacking positional characteristics; the pain remained unchanged. Neurology evaluation the same day listed tension-type headache and post–dural puncture headache as leading differentials, and she was discharged after a modest pain reduction with conservative measures. Two days later, she was readmitted with a hypertensive emergency, severe frontal headache, and laboratory abnormalities including elevated lactate dehydrogenase, elevated uric acid, and proteinuria. She was diagnosed with postpartum preeclampsia and treated with 24 hours of magnesium sulfate. Her headache persisted despite antihypertensive therapy and multiple analgesics (Fioricet, Toradol, Compazine, Neurontin, caffeine, methylprednisolone), and neurologic examination remained intact. A noncontrast head CT showed possible sphenoid sinusitis, slight prominence of the pituitary gland, intraventricular air, and tentorial dural calcification. The headache improved after blood pressure control, and she was discharged. On postpartum day 10, she returned with worsening frontal headache, neck pain, and low-grade fever; her neurologic examination remained unchanged, and a CT venogram was requested.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Post–dural puncture headache was considered because of the temporal relation to epidural analgesia but was thought less likely given absence of positional pain and lack of response to a blood patch — “although her headache lacked the traditional characteristics of postdural puncture headache (PDPH) including positional components of pain…Her headache was unchanged immediately following the procedure.”  
2. Tension-type headache was considered by neurology due to the persistent, continuous frontal pain without focal findings — “She received a neurology consultation the same day with leading differentials including tension-type headache and PDPH.”  
3. Postpartum preeclampsia was diagnosed based on new-onset hypertension, elevated lactate dehydrogenase, elevated uric acid, and proteinuria — “She was diagnosed with postpartum preeclampsia and treated with 24 hours of magnesium sulfate administration.”  
4. Sphenoid sinusitis was proposed after noncontrast CT showed possible sinus disease as a secondary headache cause — “Computed topography imaging without contrast on her second admission revealed possible sphenoid sinusitis…”  
5. Cerebral venous thrombosis was ultimately confirmed by CT venography demonstrating a filling defect in the cerebral venous sinuses — “She received a CT venogram that confirmed a filling defect in the superior sagittal sinus extending into the torcula and proximal left transverse sinus, consistent with cerebral venous thrombosis.”
